This article fits two surveys of the same region with one model: a count
survey that covers every map unit and a detection survey that covers only part
of the map. Both respond to one unmeasured spatial driver, and a copy scale
says how strongly the detection survey feels it. The article ends with
detection probabilities predicted for the units the detection survey never
visited, and with a second data set in which the two surveys share nothing.
The [Spatial models](spatial-models.html) article covers a single areal field
and is the background for this one. Installation is covered in
[Get started](tulpa.html).

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(tulpa)
```

## The model

Two response arms share the map units $s = 1, \ldots, S$. Index the
observations of the count arm by $i$ and those of the detection arm by $j$,
and let $s(i)$ and $s(j)$ denote the unit an observation was taken in. The
count arm is Poisson and the detection arm binomial with $m = 10$ trials:

$$
y_{1i} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_i), \qquad
\log \mu_i = \beta_{10} + \beta_{11} x_{1i} + \sigma z_{s(i)},
$$

$$
y_{2j} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(m, p_j), \qquad
\operatorname{logit} p_j = \beta_{20} + \beta_{21} x_{2j} + \alpha \sigma z_{s(j)}.
$$

Each arm has its own intercept and slope ($\beta_{10}, \beta_{11}$ and
$\beta_{20}, \beta_{21}$) on its own covariate. The vector $z$ holds one value
per unit and carries an intrinsic conditional autoregressive (ICAR) prior with
unit precision,

$$
p(z) \propto \exp\Big(-\tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{s \sim t} (z_s - z_t)^2\Big),
\qquad \sum_{s=1}^{S} z_s = 0,
$$

where $s \sim t$ runs over pairs of neighbouring units. The field amplitude
$\sigma$ scales $z$ in the count arm, and the copy scale $\alpha \ge 0$ scales
the same field again in the detection arm. With $\alpha = 1$ the two arms see
the field at the same strength; with $\alpha = 0$ the detection arm carries no
field at all and the two arms share nothing.

The copy scale has a prior with two parts. A point mass of probability $1/2$
sits at $\alpha = 0$, the model in which the arms are unrelated, and the other
half is spread over $\alpha > 0$ by an exponential density whose rate puts 5%
of that half above the largest node of the copy-scale axis. The posterior mass
left on the point is then the posterior probability that the arms share no
field, and because the prior odds are one, its odds are also the Bayes factor
for the uncoupled model. The amplitude $\sigma$ carries the engine's default
penalized-complexity prior, $P(\sigma > 3) = 0.01$.

`tulpa_nested_laplace_joint()` integrates $\sigma$ and $\alpha$ on an outer
grid. At each grid cell an inner Laplace approximation solves for the four
coefficients and the $S$ field values together, and the cells are weighted by
their marginal likelihood times the hyperprior. The copy-scale axis the
engine lays when the call names no nodes is:

```{r alpha-axis}
round(tulpa_grid_axis("copy_alpha"), 3)
```

The first node is the point mass. The other nine are the continuum, and the
largest, 3, sets the rate of its exponential prior.

## Simulating data

The map is an 8 by 8 lattice of units, each a neighbour of the units directly
above, below, left and right of it. The adjacency goes to the engine in
compressed sparse row form: the 0-based neighbour indices in `adj_col_idx`,
with `adj_row_ptr` marking where each unit's neighbours start.

```{r lattice}
nr <- 8L; nc <- 8L; S <- nr * nc
rc <- expand.grid(r = seq_len(nr), c = seq_len(nc))
nb <- lapply(seq_len(S), function(s)
  which(abs(rc$r - rc$r[s]) + abs(rc$c - rc$c[s]) == 1))
nn <- lengths(nb)
icar <- list(type = "icar", n_spatial_units = S,
             adj_row_ptr = c(0L, cumsum(nn)),
             adj_col_idx = unlist(nb) - 1L, n_neighbors = nn)
```

The true spatial effect `w` is a smooth surface with standard deviation 0.8
on the log scale of the counts. It stands for an unmeasured driver such as
habitat quality. The detection arm sees it at $\alpha = 0.6$ of that strength.

```{r truth}
set.seed(1)
w <- 0.8 * as.numeric(scale(sin(rc$r / 2) + cos(rc$c / 2.5)))
alpha_true <- 0.6
```

The count survey takes three counts in every unit, each with its own covariate
value, an intercept of 0.5 and a slope of 0.4. The detection survey visits 40
of the 64 units, four times each, and records how many of ten trials detected
the species, with an intercept of $-0.3$ and a slope of 0.8. The remaining 24
units have no detection data.

```{r simulate}
s1 <- rep(seq_len(S), each = 3L); x1 <- rnorm(length(s1))
y1 <- rpois(length(s1), exp(0.5 + 0.4 * x1 + w[s1]))

visited <- sort(sample(S, 40L))
s2 <- rep(visited, each = 4L); x2 <- rnorm(length(s2))
eta2 <- -0.3 + 0.8 * x2 + alpha_true * w[s2]
y2 <- rbinom(length(s2), 10L, plogis(eta2))
c(count_obs = length(y1), detection_obs = length(y2))
```

## Fitting

Each arm is a list holding its response, trial counts, design matrix,
the unit of each observation and its family. The detection arm adds
`field_coef = "alpha"`, which names the copy scale and lays it on the
default axis shown above. `store_Q = TRUE` keeps each cell's inner precision
so that posterior draws of the field can be taken afterwards.

```{r arms}
counts <- list(y = y1, n_trials = rep(1L, length(y1)),
               X = cbind(1, x = x1), spatial_idx = s1,
               family = "poisson")
detect <- list(y = y2, n_trials = rep(10L, length(y2)),
               X = cbind(1, x = x2), spatial_idx = s2,
               family = "binomial", field_coef = "alpha")
ctl <- list(n_threads = 2L, store_Q = TRUE, progress = FALSE)
```

```{r fit}
fit <- tulpa_nested_laplace_joint(
  responses = list(counts = counts, detect = detect),
  prior = icar, control = ctl)
fit
```

`summary()` gives the coefficients of both arms, prefixed by the arm name, and
the two hyperparameters with their posterior mean, standard deviation, median
and 95% interval.

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

The slopes come back near their true values of 0.4 and 0.8, with intervals
that contain them. The copy scale's interval, read from the hyperparameter
table, contains the true 0.6. The amplitude $\sigma$ is not compared with 0.8
directly: it multiplies an unscaled ICAR field, whose own standard deviation
depends on the lattice, so the comparison with the truth is made on the field
contribution $\sigma z_s$ below.

The posterior probability that the arms share no field is the mass the outer
grid leaves on $\alpha = 0$:

```{r copy-atom}
fit$copy_atom
```

## Checking the fit

`diagnostics()` grades the two approximation layers: the outer grid that
integrates $(\sigma, \alpha)$ and the inner Gaussian approximation at each
cell.

```{r diagnostics}
diagnostics(fit)
```

Both layers grade as good. The note on $\alpha$ says the grid cells on that
axis are 1.5 posterior standard deviations wide, so the endpoints of its
interval are resolved to within one cell.

A posterior predictive check compares the count arm with counts replicated
from the fit. `tulpa_posterior_draws()` samples the latent vector from the
fitted grid mixture: one row per draw, with the four coefficients first and
the 64 field values after them. Attribute `theta` holds the matching
$(\sigma, \alpha)$ of each draw.

```{r draws}
set.seed(2)
d  <- tulpa_posterior_draws(fit, n = 1000)
th <- attr(d, "theta")
zc <- fit$arm_layout$phi_start + seq_len(S)
f1 <- th[, "sigma"] * d[, zc]
f2 <- th[, "alpha"] * f1
```

`f1` holds the field contribution $\sigma z_s$ in the count arm and `f2` the
contribution $\alpha \sigma z_s$ in the detection arm, one column per unit.
The replicated variance of the counts, one value per draw, is set against the
observed variance:

```{r ppc, fig.alt = "Histogram of the variance of replicated counts across 1000 posterior draws with a vertical line at the observed variance, which sits inside the bulk of the histogram"}
eta1 <- d[, 1] + outer(d[, 2], x1) + f1[, s1]
yrep <- matrix(rpois(length(eta1), exp(eta1)), nrow = nrow(eta1))
v_rep <- apply(yrep, 1, var)
hist(v_rep, breaks = 30, main = "", xlab = "variance of replicated counts")
abline(v = var(y1), lwd = 2, col = "darkorange")
mean(v_rep >= var(y1))
```

The observed variance falls inside the replicated distribution, and the
printed share is the posterior predictive p-value of that statistic.

## Interpreting the fit

The field contribution in the count arm is set against the true effect `w`,
unit by unit, with 95% intervals from the draws.

```{r field-plot, fig.alt = "Scatter of the estimated field contribution against the true spatial effect for the 64 units, with vertical 95 percent interval bars, lying along the identity line"}
q1 <- apply(f1, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
plot(w, q1[2, ], pch = 19, ylim = range(q1),
     xlab = "true spatial effect", ylab = "estimated sigma * z")
segments(w, q1[1, ], w, q1[3, ], col = "grey60")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
c(correlation = cor(q1[2, ], w), sd_estimate = sd(q1[2, ]))
```

The estimates lie along the identity line with a correlation of 0.97. Their
standard deviation is 0.68 against the true 0.8: the ICAR prior pulls each
unit toward its neighbours, which shrinks the extremes of the surface.

The posterior of the copy scale is read from the outer grid.
`tulpa_outer_grid()` returns one row per cell with its $(\sigma, \alpha)$
value in `nodes` and its normalized weight in `weights`. Summing the weights
over the cells at each $\alpha$ level gives that axis's marginal.

```{r grid}
g <- tulpa_outer_grid(fit)
dim(g$nodes)
p_alpha <- tapply(g$weights, g$nodes[, "alpha"], sum)
round(p_alpha, 3)
```

The grid holds more $\alpha$ levels than the default axis, because the fit's
refinement added levels between 0.44 and 0.75, where the posterior sits. The
point mass at zero carries no weight.

```{r alpha-plot, fig.alt = "Bar chart of the posterior weight on each level of the copy scale alpha, with the level at zero empty and the weight concentrated between about 0.45 and 0.85"}
lev <- as.numeric(names(p_alpha))
plot(lev, p_alpha, type = "h", lwd = 4, xlim = c(0, 1.5),
     xlab = "copy scale alpha", ylab = "posterior weight")
abline(v = alpha_true, lty = 2)
```

## What the shared field buys

The same detection data, fitted alone, carries its own field with its own
amplitude and no information from the counts. A joint fit with one arm is
that model.

```{r fit-separate}
detect_alone <- detect
detect_alone$field_coef <- NULL
fit_d <- tulpa_nested_laplace_joint(
  responses = list(detect = detect_alone), prior = icar, control = ctl)
rbind(joint = confint(fit)["detect.x", ],
      separate = confint(fit_d)["detect.x", ])
```

The slope intervals are nearly the same width. The difference is in the field.
At the 24 units the detection survey never visited, the separate fit can only
interpolate from neighbouring units, while the joint fit also reads the
counts taken there.

```{r field-unvisited}
set.seed(3)
dd <- tulpa_posterior_draws(fit_d, n = 1000)
fd <- attr(dd, "theta")[, "sigma"] * dd[, fit_d$arm_layout$phi_start + seq_len(S)]
unvisited <- setdiff(seq_len(S), visited)
err <- function(f) sqrt(mean((colMeans(f[, unvisited]) -
                               alpha_true * w[unvisited])^2))
wid <- function(f) mean(apply(f[, unvisited], 2, function(v)
  diff(quantile(v, c(0.025, 0.975)))))
rbind(joint = c(rmse = err(f2), interval_width = wid(f2)),
      separate = c(rmse = err(fd), interval_width = wid(fd)))
```

On these 24 units the root mean squared error of the detection-arm field is
0.11 for the joint fit and 0.25 for the separate fit, with intervals of
similar width.

## Prediction

The detection probability at an unvisited unit, for a covariate value of zero,
is $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_{20} + \alpha \sigma z_s)$. Each posterior
draw gives one value, so the draws carry the uncertainty of the intercept, the
copy scale and the field together.

```{r predict}
p_joint <- plogis(d[, 3] + f2[, unvisited])
p_sep   <- plogis(dd[, 1] + fd[, unvisited])
p_true  <- plogis(-0.3 + alpha_true * w[unvisited])
qj <- apply(p_joint, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
qs <- apply(p_sep,   2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
```

```{r predict-plot, fig.alt = "Predicted detection probability at the 24 unvisited units, ordered by the true probability, with 95 percent intervals for the joint and the separate fit and the truth as crosses; the joint intervals follow the truth while the separate ones stay near the average"}
o <- order(p_true); k <- seq_along(o)
plot(k - 0.15, qj[2, o], pch = 19, ylim = range(qj, qs),
     xlab = "unvisited unit (ordered by true probability)",
     ylab = "detection probability at x = 0")
segments(k - 0.15, qj[1, o], k - 0.15, qj[3, o])
points(k + 0.15, qs[2, o], pch = 1, col = "steelblue")
segments(k + 0.15, qs[1, o], k + 0.15, qs[3, o], col = "steelblue")
points(k, p_true[o], pch = 4, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("joint", "separate", "truth"), pch = c(19, 1, 4),
       col = c("black", "steelblue", "darkorange"), bty = "n")
```

The joint predictions rise with the true probability across the unvisited
units. The separate predictions move less, because only the neighbouring
visited units inform them.

## Model comparison

`logLik()` on a joint fit returns the log evidence: the marginal likelihood
integrated over the outer grid with the hyperpriors. Two restricted models are
compared with the copy model. With `field_coef = 0` the detection arm carries
no field; with `field_coef = 1` it carries the field at the count arm's
strength. Both fit only $\sigma$ on the outer grid.

```{r compare}
detect_0 <- detect; detect_0$field_coef <- 0
detect_1 <- detect; detect_1$field_coef <- 1
fit_0 <- tulpa_nested_laplace_joint(list(counts = counts, detect = detect_0),
                                    prior = icar, control = ctl)
fit_1 <- tulpa_nested_laplace_joint(list(counts = counts, detect = detect_1),
                                    prior = icar, control = ctl)
compare_models(copy = fit, no_field = fit_0, alpha_one = fit_1,
               criterion = "loglik")
```

The model with no field in the detection arm sits 37.5 log units below the
copy model. The model with $\alpha$ fixed at 1 sits 1.6 below it, so the data
prefer a detection arm that feels the field more weakly than the count arm. The separate fit
`fit_d` does not enter this table, because it models only the detection data
and its evidence is on a different set of observations.

## When the arms share nothing

The second data set keeps the counts and replaces the detections by data
simulated with $\alpha = 0$: the detection arm has its covariate effect and
no spatial field.

```{r fit-zero}
set.seed(4)
detect_z <- detect
detect_z$y <- rbinom(length(s2), 10L, plogis(-0.3 + 0.8 * x2))
fit_z <- tulpa_nested_laplace_joint(list(counts = counts, detect = detect_z),
                                    prior = icar, control = ctl)
fit_z$copy_atom
```

The point mass now holds 0.90 of the posterior weight on $\alpha$. The
warning concerns the continuum part of the axis: its own weight piles up at
its smallest node, 0.1, as the per-level weights show.

```{r zero-levels}
gz <- tulpa_outer_grid(fit_z)
round(tapply(gz$weights, gz$nodes[, "alpha"], sum), 3)
```

Because the prior odds are one, the posterior odds on the point mass are the
Bayes factor for the model with no shared field:

```{r bayes-factor}
pm <- fit_z$copy_atom$posterior_mass
c(posterior_mass = pm, bayes_factor_uncoupled = pm / (1 - pm))
```

The data favour the uncoupled model by a factor of about 9.

## A weak second arm

How much the detection arm can say about $\alpha$ depends on how much
information it carries. Refitting the first data set with each detection
reduced to a single binary trial, still at the true $\alpha = 0.6$:

```{r fit-weak}
set.seed(5)
detect_w <- detect
detect_w$n_trials <- rep(1L, length(s2))
detect_w$y <- rbinom(length(s2), 1L, plogis(eta2))
fit_w <- tulpa_nested_laplace_joint(list(counts = counts, detect = detect_w),
                                    prior = icar, control = ctl)
fit_w$copy_atom
fit_w$theta_ci_lo["alpha"]; fit_w$theta_ci_hi["alpha"]
```

With 160 binary detections the 95% interval for $\alpha$ runs from 0.32 to
1.38, against 0.50 to 0.87 with ten trials per detection, and the point mass
still holds almost no weight. The weaker arm leaves the coupling detected but
its strength poorly resolved.

## Practical guidance

- **Read `copy_atom` with its prior.** The point at $\alpha = 0$ starts with
  probability 1/2, so the posterior mass on it reads directly as a posterior
  probability, and its odds as a Bayes factor. Here it was 0 at
  $\alpha = 0.6$ and 0.90 at $\alpha = 0$.
- **The arm with less information decides how well $\alpha$ is resolved.**
  With 160 detections of ten trials each the 95% interval for $\alpha$ was
  0.37 wide; with 160 single trials it was 1.06 wide. A large
  `posterior_mass` is evidence for "no shared field" only if the weaker arm
  could have shown one; simulating from the fitted model at a plausible
  $\alpha$ checks that.
- **A railed warning beside a heavy point mass is about the continuum.** When
  most of the weight sits at $\alpha = 0$, the remainder piles up at the
  smallest continuum node and the fit warns that $\alpha$ lies on its lower
  edge. `copy_atom` and the per-level weights from `tulpa_outer_grid()` show
  how the mass is split.
- **The gain from sharing is largest where one arm has no data.** On the
  24 units without detections the field error fell from 0.25 to 0.11; the
  slope interval of the detection arm barely changed. A joint model pays off for mapping and
  prediction across the gaps of the sparser survey.
- **$\alpha$ is non-negative.** The copy scale scales the donor field and
  cannot flip its sign, so a driver that raises one response and lowers the
  other is not represented. Fixed multipliers are set with a numeric
  `field_coef`, as in the comparison above.
- **One arm carries the copy scale on a single shared field.** For several
  shared fields, each copied onto its own arm with its own $\alpha$, pass a
  list of prior blocks and the `copy` argument (`?tulpa_nested_laplace_joint`).
- **Compare $\sigma$ on the field scale.** The amplitude multiplies an
  unscaled ICAR field; the field contribution $\sigma z_s$, drawn with
  `tulpa_posterior_draws()`, is the quantity to compare across lattices or
  with a simulated truth.
- **Use a joint model only when the arms are measured on the same units.**
  The field is indexed by unit; two surveys of different regions, or of the
  same region at unrelated resolutions, have no shared index to align.
